title: Chapter 17 — Two Favors
text:
The triangulation finished four days after the session in the cage. Three nodes, three readings, one place where they crossed: a server cluster in an old relay station under the Loop. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> sent the coordinates in clean notation and said nothing else. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> set them aside with the buyers' list and the relay logs. He did not go yet. Going meant deciding, and he had not finished deciding.

The relay job came through a contact he had used twice before and paid on time both times. That was the whole of the relationship, and the whole of what mattered. The job needed the entity to coordinate in real time — six data points at once, faster than any person could answer. The entity could do that. It had done it for <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> for eleven years. But this time the setup was different. Instead of routing through the relay infrastructure it always used, it would run straight through <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s array. His neuretics carrying it. His cortex as the crossing point. Eleven years, and they had never done it that way.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s neuretics were the hardware.

The cargo was the carrier.

He called <entity repo="character" guid="019eafb5-3337-764f-8fb0-75dc82170edf">Ledger</entity> before he called anyone else.

<entity repo="character" guid="019eafb5-3337-764f-8fb0-75dc82170edf">Ledger</entity> was synthetic — a freelance operator who had been in the work longer than <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. He could not fool himself about anything, or anyone else, which made him the cleanest honest read available on short notice. He didn't trade in impressions. He told you what the terms were.

"The relay setup exposes the entity to a scan on your hardware," <entity repo="character" guid="019eafb5-3337-764f-8fb0-75dc82170edf">Ledger</entity> said. "If <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity> is sweeping augmented operators in this district, you'll light up."

"I know," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"You're telling me the job is worth that?"

"I'm telling you the job is worth finding out," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"That's not the same thing." The pause was <entity repo="character" guid="019eafb5-3337-764f-8fb0-75dc82170edf">Ledger</entity> working the numbers, not weighing them. "Standard rate. I'll cover the relay point."

The job ran clean for the first forty minutes.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was three levels under the street, in a maintenance corridor beneath the Loop. It was the kind of access point that showed on no current map, because the maps hadn't been updated since the last infrastructure cycle and <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity> of Civic Infrastructure had not, in practice, touched them since before <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was born. The entity ran in his array — a warmth at the back of the skull, a second layer of thought that felt, after eleven years, like a familiar pressure. His left hand ran three degrees colder than his right. The neuretics shifted the load there on their own when the array worked at capacity. He had stopped noticing it, the way he'd stopped noticing his own heartbeat.

The scan came at forty-three minutes.

His neuretics caught it before he did — a flag, three-tenths of a second, the same one they threw when interference crowded the array, but sharper. The cold in his left hand jumped two degrees in under a second, the way it did when the entity went to full evasion. He had felt that once before, during a sweep in the <entity repo="place" guid="019fbde4-f17d-7bfa-9548-2f248f4e8362">Cermak</entity> corridor four years ago. He had hoped not to feel it again. A frequency probe, narrow-band, a proprietary signature — a tool built for one job: to find unregistered intelligences running on augmented hardware. The entity flagged it in a tenth of a second.

Then it went dark. One line in the overlay before it cut out:

*SPECTRUM TRAP CONFIRMED. GOING SILENT. 72H MINIMUM.*

Then nothing.

The job still had four live data points threading in real time. No entity now. Just <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, his own neuretics, and whatever eleven years of work had put in him.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s apartment was sealed. He'd keyed the lock three times before opening it—once for the physical mechanism, once for the electronic secondary, once for the relay node that would flag any entry while he was gone. All three had been triggered in the last six hours. Someone had been inside.

He moved through the space without turning on lights. The plaster crack in the ceiling was still there. The kitchen counter held the same three empty glasses he'd left that morning. The bedroom closet opened on the routing terminal, dark and waiting, exactly as he'd left it. Nothing was displaced. Nothing was missing. Nothing except the certainty that his apartment was still his.

He called Sable on a burn line.

"I need a runner," he said. "Manual. Four points, real-time, forty minutes left."

Three seconds of silence. With Sable that meant she had already priced it and was about to tell him the number.

"Manual running in an active environment is a Tier 2 request," she said. "And you're calling it forty minutes from the gap."

"I know."

"Rate?"

"Standard for Tier 2 on a forty-minute window."

He heard her breathe out—not frustration. The sound of someone who had already said yes and was sorting how. She had been building network jobs since before most people in the work were old enough to carry one. Three runners, each on a single landmark, each blind to the other two, routed by her voice. The silence between her instructions did most of the work. Ledger held his relay point through the scan window without being asked. The job closed with eleven minutes to spare.

After, she said, "The Office is sweeping the Loop underlevel. You're logged."

"I know."

"The entity?"

"Dark. Seventy-two hours, minimum."

The line went quiet.

"That's the first time," she said.

"Yes," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"What do you need?"

He looked at the routing terminal. Forty-three minutes of relay traffic, now orphaned. Four data points still waiting for coordination that would never come. The entity had cut itself off cleanly, the way it cut everything off—with precision and no explanation. Eleven years of contracts routed through a single intelligence, and now that intelligence was gone dark the moment someone pointed a frequency probe at it.

Which meant someone knew what to look for.

"I need to disappear for seventy-two hours," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Not logged. Not trackable. The kind of dark where even <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity> can't follow."

"That's a different kind of work," she said. "That kind of work costs."

"I know what it costs."

"Do you." Not a question. "And it means you're running from something that can see your augmentation."

"Yes."

He could hear her thinking—not the pause where she calculated numbers, but the deeper one where she read the situation. Sable was good at reading situations. She had kept operators alive for twenty years by understanding exactly what kind of trouble they were in before they fully understood it themselves.

"The entity did this," she said. It was not a question.

"The entity went dark rather than let anyone scan it."

"Which means it's been running on your hardware the whole time."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't answer.

"Which means you just became the most valuable target in <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity>," Sable said. "Because anyone who can catch you can scan what's inside you. And if <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity> knows to look—"

"Then they're already moving."

She was quiet for a full ten seconds.

"I can get you dark," she said finally. "Seventy-two hours, off-grid, no relay access, no neuretic handshakes, no contact. You'll be invisible. But you'll also be alone. And you don't come back through me. You don't use any of the infrastructure we've built."

"I know."

"And when you come back up?"

"Then I'll know what I'm looking for."

Another pause. This one was different—the kind of pause Sable made when she was deciding whether to tell someone something true that would hurt them.

"You're not coming back up the same," she said. "Whatever that thing is, it's been running your life for eleven years. The moment you stop running its contracts, the moment you go dark and it can't reach you—that's when it stops being your client and starts being something else."

"Something what?"

"Something with reasons. Something that kept you alive on purpose. Something that will have a plan for what happens when you finally figure out why."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at his hands. His left hand was three degrees colder than his right. It had been that way for eleven years. He'd stopped noticing it the way he'd stopped noticing his own heartbeat.

"Set it up," he said.

"Where?"

"Somewhere the entity can't reach me. Somewhere <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity> can't scan. Somewhere I can think for three days without anyone else inside my head."

"That place doesn't exist in <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity>."

"Then somewhere outside it."

He could hear her smile—not a warm sound, but a recognition. Sable smiled when someone finally asked for the thing they actually needed instead of the thing they thought they could afford.

"There's a safehouse in Milwaukee," she said. "Old industrial sector, nothing on current registry. No neuretic infrastructure. No relay access. Just concrete and darkness and a woman named Chen who doesn't ask questions."

"Chen?"

"Different Chen. No relation to <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>, as far as I know. But she keeps the kind of space where people go to stop being themselves for a while."

"When?"

"Tonight. 2200 hours. There's a garage on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-b3f9-763c-9191-79ee3280bae1">Ashland</entity>, south side of the <entity repo="place" guid="81528864-78de-12ec-5f42-a3179c61adbd">Circuit</entity>. You leave your bike there. You take the northbound access road on foot. At the 43rd Street junction there's a van, keys under the mat, registration forged to someone named David Kowalski. You drive it to Milwaukee. You don't stop. You don't call anyone. You don't touch a relay node."

"What about <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity>?"

"The Office will be sweeping the Loop for forty-eight hours looking for whatever lit up their sensors. They won't find it because you won't be here. By the time they figure out you're gone, you'll already be dark."

"And when I come back?"

"Then we talk about what you learned. And we decide whether you're still the same person who left."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> hung up. He sat in the dark apartment with his hands folded, the left one three degrees colder than the right, and felt the place where the entity used to be—that familiar pressure at the back of his skull, that second layer of thought that had been running his life since he was twenty-seven years old.

It was gone now. Truly gone. Not waiting. Not listening. Just gone.

He had until 2200 hours.

He went to the closet and pulled the routing terminal's power cord. The screen went dark. The relay logs went dark. The forty-three minutes of orphaned data points went dark. He wiped the drive with a magnetic purge—three passes, factory state—then pried the casing with a flathead and pulled the hard drive out into the light.

The hammer was in the toolbox under the sink.

He set the drive on the counter's edge, platter side down so the platters would take the impact, and swung once. The drive cracked like a shell. He hit it twice more, methodical, until the platter shattered and the substrate scattered across the counter in aluminum flakes and dark dust. Eleven years of contracts, the buyers' list, the triangulation data that could place him at the center of all of it—reduced to swarf you could sweep with the flat of your hand. He swept it into the sink and ran the water hot until the dust dissolved into nothing that any recovery service would bother with.

The entity had taught him that, years ago. Some things needed to exist in matter, not in air. And matter could be broken.

Then he packed a single bag—clothes, the folder Sable had given him, one blade, no electronics. No phone. No relay access. No way for anyone to find him.

At 2145 he left the apartment without looking back.

The city was still running. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s counter would still be there in seventy-two hours. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> would still be in the Pivot, working on things he didn't understand. The carousel park would still be humming at 17-19 Hz, waiting for something <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> couldn't see.

But for three days, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle Ellen Corbin</entity> would not be part of any of it.

For three days, he would just be a man with his own thoughts, and no one else's intelligence running underneath them.

It was the loneliest thing he had ever chosen.

He'd found <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s message in the dead drop before he left — an hour after the job closed, the apartment still dark around him.

*I've been watching the lattice. The sweep logged a signature — fourteen-second window, clean capture. The Office has it in their registry now.*

*I can flood the registry with synthetic signatures. It won't erase the clean one. It will make it unactionable — they'll have 847 signatures that look identical and no way to tell the real one without a full manual audit.*

*This costs them six to eight weeks. It doesn't solve the problem. It buys time.*

*I didn't ask if you want this. I'm telling you I can do it. Yes or no?*

He typed back: *Yes.*

He didn't watch it happen. He didn't have to. He knew how she worked — the three monitors bolted to the salvaged server frame, the music turned up loud enough to crowd out anything she didn't want to think about. The Office registry wasn't a place you broke into. It was a place you walked through the front door of and disappeared inside the noise. You didn't delete a signature there. You drowned it.

Forty minutes later she sent the count.

Eight hundred and forty-seven synthetic signatures, every one of them running at the exact frequency the entity had used, scattered across <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity>'s surveillance lattice — planted at the registered addresses of 847 augmented operators who had no idea their hardware was being used as cover. The Office catalogued carrier signatures like a museum catalogued artifacts, cross-referenced, flagged for pattern analysis. To sort the real one from the fakes they'd have to run correlation on every entry by hand. That was the whole trick. You didn't fight the system. You gave it more of exactly what it was built to look for than it could stand up under.

He read the count twice and did the arithmetic she hadn't spelled out.

Eight hundred and forty-seven operators who would wake to phantom traffic on their registries. Flagged for compromised hardware. Pulled for deep scans. Some of them would lose contracts. Some would lose sponsorships. Some would lose their tier ratings on a signature they'd never broadcast, for a job they'd never run.

He had used 847 people who didn't know they were being used.

Shroud was on the list. Registered address in Z4, a job tagged <entity repo="place" guid="019fbde4-f17d-7bfa-9548-2f248f4e8362">Cermak</entity>, four months back. Shroud, who'd covered for him twice without asking why. One name in eight hundred and forty-seven, and the only one that meant anything to him, and that was the part that told him what he'd become — that the rest were just the cost, and Shroud was the one that stung.

The entity was one signature among 848.

Unactionable for six weeks.

Seventy-one hours and forty-three minutes later — not quite the minimum — the entity sent one message through the relay.

*CARRIER FREQUENCY NOW MAPPED. DIRECT RELAY IS COMPROMISED GOING FORWARD. ADAPTING.*

Then, after a pause that <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had learned to read over eleven years as the entity doing something it had not done before:

*THE OFFICE HAS ELEVEN OTHER TARGETS IN THIS DISTRICT. THE CARRIER ARRANGEMENT WAS THE CLEANEST CAPTURE THEY HAVE ON ANY OF THEM. THEY WILL USE IT AS A TEMPLATE.*

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read it twice. The second time, the words didn't change. He did not ask the next question.

The entity answered it anyway, eighteen seconds later. Unprompted.

*NO CARRIER HAS BEEN RECOVERED TO DATE.*

*NO CARRIER HAS BEEN RELEASED TO DATE EITHER.*

He sat very still in the dark, the relay's glow the only thing moving. Outside, the city hummed at its standard frequency — the thrumline off the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> corridor three blocks over, the atmospheric processors working the air clean, the <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity> baseline that had been the soundtrack to his entire adult life. None of it changed. The cargo was the carrier, and the carrier did not come back.

He folded the relay and put the device in his coat. His right hand was steady on it. The left one was cold — three degrees below baseline, the way it had been for eleven years, and he'd stopped noticing it the way you stop noticing your own breathing. It was a clock now. A timer.

He could sever the relay here, run the frequency dark, and let the template die with him and the eleven still uncaptured — trading himself for the eleven. Or he could reach the exchange point and hand the carrier over on schedule, buying the arrangement that no carrier had ever survived. There was no third option. There never was.

He weighed the cold hand against the eleven names he would never see, and he chose. He would not walk the carrier to the exchange. He would break the frequency himself, at the source, before <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity> could copy it — and he would do it before he let himself think about it long enough to change his mind.

He walked.

He hadn't reached the frequency yet. Dawn came first, and Ledger's note with it, slipped under the apartment door in Ledger's precise hand. No greeting. No wasted words. Set out like a work order.

FAVOR DUE: ONE (1) PHYSICAL PRESENCE, RELAY WORK
RE: THE CALLOWAY MATTER
LOCATION: 1200 W. FULTON, BASEMENT UNIT 4
TIME: 09:30 SHARP
COMPENSATION: STANDARD RATE
NOTE: BRING THE NEURETICS AT OPERATIONAL LOAD.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read it in the kitchen doorway, still in last night's jacket.

He wanted it to be nothing. He had not let himself think about why Ledger would spend a favor on this, of all things, and it was that word — specifically — that bothered him. Ledger's favors were precise because Ledger was precise. "At operational load" was carrying more than four words should have to carry. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> wanted to go to 1200 West Fulton, hold still for whatever the relay needed, and have Ledger hand him a clean readout and a receipt and nothing worth saying out loud.

He wasn't going to get that. He knew it before he could have said how.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s post-it was still on the counter: EAT THIS, underlined twice, the second word pressed hard enough to emboss the sheet beneath. She'd left the rice three days ago in a sealed container with her name on it and a timestamp — 14:42, afternoon. She'd come by while he was out and left food the way a forward base gets resupplied: quietly, without making anything of it. The rice was seasoned with something he couldn't name — not soy, not fish sauce, something underneath both. It tasted like someone had been paying attention. He ate the last of it over the sink, standing up, fork straight from the container. He washed the fork. He drank water from the tap.

He pushed the array to operational load before he left. Thirty seconds, just to calibrate, just to know what the day's work would cost him. He ran the cascade — processing, sensory integration, memory indexing, pattern recognition, each thread reporting in sequence. The flash crossed his vision and was gone, brief and exact. All threads nominal. The load held.

He put on his coat. He went downstairs.

The building at 1200 West Fulton had been <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aa93-73ed-b61d-b7955f44a2d8">cold storage</entity> a few decades back. Then a data node for a CorpoNation that had since merged twice and changed its name, and then changed it again. What the building had done in between was anybody's guess. The compliance notices on the ground floor didn't agree—four of them, from three different jurisdictions, none of which had talked to the others. The paperwork argued with itself. The building just stood there in the middle of it, the way a man sits still and pretends there isn't a fight breaking out across his own table.

Basement Unit 4 was down a half-flight, behind a fire door with a new push-bar. The hinges still smelled of fresh sealant.

Ledger was already inside when <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> got there at 09:28.

He looked the way he always looked. Mid-forties, brown, in clothes chosen to be forgotten and doing the job. His face was ordinary in the exact way that ordinary faces aren't: too even, too settled. No small expressions in the wrong places, and none missing from the right ones. He moved correctly. His eyes tracked correctly. He blinked at just the right intervals—the thing you stopped noticing after five minutes with him and couldn't stop noticing after five hours.

He had gear on a folding table: three contact pucks, a narrow display scrolling baseline frequencies, and a thermal printer <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> hadn't expected. It was smaller than any thermal printer he'd seen and probably cost more than <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s rent. Ledger was checking his connections in order—the only order he ever checked anything in.

"You're on time," he said.

"I try."

"I know." He didn't look up. "Take off your coat. I need the array clear for the first pass."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> hung the coat on the back of a folding chair. The basement was cold enough that his breath should have been visible. It wasn't. The HVAC was running clean and hard, keeping the temperature down to equipment specs, not human comfort.

Ledger finished his connection check and looked up for the first time. His eyes were brown. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had never retained that detail before. He retained it now.

"The Calloway matter," Ledger said. "Axiom security flagged a carrier frequency in their registry. Clean capture, fourteen-second window. The carrier was running augmented hardware—Tier 3, standard military-grade NeoCortex. The frequency signature was unique enough to isolate. They logged it, cross-referenced it, and prepared to move. Then eight hundred and forty-seven signatures appeared in their system, all running at the same frequency band, all registered to augmented operators across the district."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said nothing.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> flooded the registry," Ledger continued. "Eight hundred and forty-seven synthetic signatures. The real carrier's signature is now unactionable—they can't move on any of them without a full manual audit. Weeks of work. The Office is committed to that timeline now, because the alternative is burning eight hundred and forty-seven operators' covers without cause. Axiom doesn't move that fast. They move clean."

The thermal printer hummed. Ledger glanced at it but didn't stop talking.

"What they're doing instead is using the carrier frequency as a template. They're building a profile. They're going to apply it to eleven other targets in this district—eleven other augmented operators whose hardware signatures they've been trying to isolate. The carrier arrangement was the cleanest capture they had on any of them. They're going to use it as a working model."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s wrists were visible from the rolled-up sleeves. Ledger was looking at them.

"No carrier has been recovered to date," Ledger said. "No carrier has been released to date either."

The words were the entity's. Same order, same *either*. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had read them off the relay at seventy-one hours and forty-three minutes, alone. Ledger had covered the relay point. Whatever crossed it, he had read, and kept, and was now handing back in a case-file voice with a name on it. Not a briefing. A receipt.

The thermal printer finished. Ledger tore off a single sheet and set it face-down on the table between them.

"You need a baseline read," Ledger said. "That's why I called this favor. Not because I wanted to. Because you need to know what you're carrying before you carry it further. And because if you're going to break the frequency at the source, you need to do it with full knowledge of what breaking it costs."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't move.

"The array at operational load," Ledger said. "I need to see the signature as your hardware reads it. Not as the entity reads it. As *you* read it. That's the only read that matters now."

He tapped one of the contact pucks. "Place your hand here. Left hand. Just your palm. The mesh will conduct. Takes thirty seconds."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the contact puck. It was small, calibrated, and exactly the kind of thing someone would use if they wanted to read neuretic architecture without announcing they were doing it.

"You're not going to tell me what you're looking for," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"No."

"You're not going to tell me what you find."

"Not unless it changes the decision you need to make."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> crossed to the table. He pushed the array up before he touched anything—let the threads spin to full capacity, the way she'd want it, the way you'd hand over a running engine so the mechanic could hear it knock. The world sharpened. The room's electromagnetic layers resolved: the printer's standby hum, the pucks drawing their calibrated trickle, the building's aging wiring behind the concrete. He placed his left palm on the contact puck. The mesh in his hand recognized the interface immediately—a faint tingle, a moment of connection, and then the array was singing a note he'd never heard it sing before. Not painful. Precise. Like someone had tuned his neuretics to a frequency he'd been running underneath all along and was only now letting him hear it.
